title: A scientist shared unpublished research with Claude. Now he’s questioning an AI discovery
source_used: Yahoo Tech (syndicated from Cult of Mac, per its affiliate-link line)
key_facts: Mario Rodriguez Mestre, a computational biology PhD candidate at the University of Copenhagen, says he shared unpublished research with Claude before Anthropic announced its findings.
He questions whether his material could have influenced the discovery; the article says there is no evidence establishing this.
Anthropic announced on 23 Sep 2026 a system it calls array-associated reverse transcriptases (ARTs), found in bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria.

About 950 Claude-powered agents searched DNA sequence data for 21 hours; Claude identified a larger arrangement of repeated DNA and an additional protein of unknown role that resembles features of CRISPR.
According to The Scientist, Mestre and colleagues had worked on the proteins for years and identified the enzyme before the announcement.
Anthropic says Claude was not trained on user transcripts and its molecular biology team had no access to Mestre's conversations; its researchers used previously published data.
Nature reported on 8 Oct 2026 that some scientists fear AI companies could announce findings before researchers on the same problem publish.
quote_evidence: Without evidence connecting Mestre's conversations to the discovery, it remains unclear whether his unpublished work played a role.
Anthropic has said Claude was not trained on user transcripts and that its molecular biology team did not have access to Mestre's conversations.
For now, the system's functions remain unclear, and there is no verified evidence that Mestre's conversations contributed to Claude's discovery.
why_it_matters_hint: Researchers who paste unpublished work into chatbots now face questions about data handling and credit.
event_date: Anthropic announcement 23 Sep 2026; Mestre's questioning reported 9 Oct 2026
